Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
never allow myself to feel or express anger
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you

vignette: The night that changed Alex's life began with a quiet argument that escalated into physical violence. The force of his partner's blows left him trembling and, in the moments that followed, he was flooded with a raw sense of fear that seemed to seep into his bones. From that night onward, ordinary movements felt charged: the screech of a bus door, the hum of a crowded station, the sight of a man standing too close. Each of these cues instantly dredged up the memory of that night, and in the flash of recollection he slipped into a pattern of self-blame rumination, suppressed anger, and a refusal to eat. His growing belief that he was inherently unsafe-his fear of harm and mistrust-only amplified the way ordinary bus rides and brief encounters with men turned into trigger moments. The memory of the abuse was not a distant echo; it unfolded as if it were happening again. Each flash was so vivid that Alex felt the same physical pain he had endured when the fists struck, and the emotional overwhelm was so intense that he had to stop, breathe, and pull back from the scene. That vividness made everyday interactions feel like threats, and it turned even the simple act of stepping onto a bus into a new trigger. The memory's persistence kept him hypervigilant to any scenario that could echo the abuse, and the constant resurfacing reinforced his sense of inadequacy, fear of harm, and mistrust of people around him. Because Alex could not trust safety, even when others assured him that he was protected, he developed a pervasive sense of threat whenever something took longer than expected. The longer a bus waited, the more he imagined danger looming; the delay felt like a warning that something bad was about to happen. This heightened sense of threat, in turn, reinforced his belief that he could never be safe, deepening his mistrust and his conviction that he was inadequate. The cycle of threat and negative appraisal grew tighter as each new delay intensified his anxiety. The self-blame, the anger that he never allowed himself to feel, and the chronic under-eating all fed into his negative appraisal of himself. Each time he tried to eat, he felt shame, and the silence of his anger left him feeling powerless and inadequate. The constant self-criticism and emotional suppression only made his sense of inadequacy grow, creating a loop that seemed impossible to break. At work, Alex is a journalist in a newsroom dominated by a handful of senior editors, most of whom are men. When a male photographer stands too close during a break, Alex avoids the break room entirely, choosing instead to sit at a desk with the window open. Even the daily commute by bus, once a source of routine, now feels like a minefield of potential triggers, forcing him to cancel assignments that require a long bus ride or to take the subway instead. These occupational avoidance behaviors have reduced his coverage opportunities and strained his relationships with colleagues. After months of self-imposed isolation and a sharp decline in his journalistic output, Alex finally sought therapy. He fears that if he continues to hide, he will lose his credibility and his relationship, yet he hopes to reclaim his voice and learn to trust safety again.
